In the demo, a cross-platform web app's global.json specified SDK 10.0.100 with a roll-forward policy, so dotnetup rolled forward to the latestFeature band; changing the policy to latestPatch caused dotnetup to install the 100 feature band (1xx) instead, and it explained that the choice came from the global.json. With one command the developer was ready to build and run the app using the correct SDK.

mentions.sessionTitle: Designing Reliable Multi‑Agent Apps with Azure Cosmos DB
mentions.shortDescription: Auto-syncing secondary containers partitioned for different access patterns, converting cross-partition queries into single-partition lookups
mentions.longDescription: Global secondary indexes are now generally available. They let you create a secondary container partitioned for different access patterns (for example, partitioned on destination) that automatically syncs data from a source container into a copy better suited for your query patterns. This transforms heavy cross-partition queries—like counting all trips to Paris across tenants—into single-partition lookups, increases query efficiency, and isolates heavy workload operations so they don't impact the transactional workload. When defining a GSI you can project only the most important properties, filtering out fields like the days array to match how you query the data.

mentions.sessionTitle: Taking your AI to the edge with .NET MAUI
mentions.rawName: Global XAML namespaces and implicit namespaces
mentions.shortDescription: Reduce or eliminate XMLNS declarations, with editor/language-service support now available
mentions.longDescription: As part of a big XAML investment in .NET 10, global namespaces were introduced so developers can reduce or completely eliminate XMLNS declarations in their projects, making XAML documents much less verbose. Implicit namespaces are in preview, and the language service and editor support that was announced as coming at .NET Conf in November is now available. The team encourages developers to try it and report feedback.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse
mentions.rawName: GPU-accelerated data warehouse / Query Acceleration (limited preview)
mentions.shortDescription: A new engine executes queries or query portions directly on GPUs, requiring no query rewrites and applying to every SQL endpoint and warehouse in a workspace once enabled.
mentions.longDescription: The Fabric DW team built a GPU-accelerated data warehouse in Fabric, purpose-built for modern AI workloads, that accelerates analytics and AI by executing queries directly on GPUs to process complex, large-scale queries more efficiently. It requires no rearchitecting, no query rewrites, and no separate systems to manage, while delivering faster, more consistent results across analytics queries, reports, AI scenarios, and analytical applications. It is built for enterprise scale and reliability, handling high concurrency and large data volumes with predictable performance, and applies broadly across agents, applications, and workloads.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: Using NVIDIA accelerated computing to deliver up to 7x query performance with no application changes
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft announced GPU acceleration for the Fabric data warehouse, built on NVIDIA accelerated computing. By combining accelerated computing with parallel processing, query performance can be increased by up to 7 times. A key point is that this high-speed data warehouse can be realized without changing the existing application running on Fabric.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering the next AI frontier with a unified data platform
mentions.rawName: GPU query acceleration for Fabric Data Warehouse (limited preview)
mentions.shortDescription: Demonstrated up to 8x faster single queries and over 100x at 64 concurrent queries, enabled via a one-click workspace setting.
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft announced the limited preview of query acceleration in the Fabric Data Warehouse through GPUs, enabled with a simple one-click setup. On TPC-H benchmarks the GPU-accelerated warehouse delivered an average 8X performance improvement over the CPU-powered Fabric Data Warehouse for single queries, and acceleration improved to roughly 25 times faster when running 16 concurrent queries. A demo later showed roughly 89% of queries were accelerated for a given warehouse.

mentions.sessionTitle: Imagine Cup World Championship
mentions.shortDescription: Microsoft surprised the finalists by raising the award on stage.
mentions.longDescription: As a surprise to the finalists, Microsoft announced that it was backing the founders more than ever before by raising the Imagine Cup grand prize from $100,000 to $150,000. The increase was revealed on stage just before the World Champion was named.

mentions.sessionTitle: Fabric IQ: Bringing enterprise intelligence into the developer workflow
mentions.rawName: Graph analytics in Fabric IQ is generally available
mentions.shortDescription: Native graph capabilities built on OneLake data and the ontology, with a visual no-code GQL query builder for multi-hop relationship and causal analysis without additional ETL
mentions.longDescription: Graph capabilities in Fabric IQ are generally available, taking the power of OneLake data and the ontology to power relationship and causal analysis. Using a visual no-code query builder, users can construct rich GQL queries without writing code, selecting nodes like entrances, course segments, and seating sections and filtering to get fast graph results. This enables understanding the implications of events at one entity (e.g., an entrance) on related areas such as a seating section, with results viewable in diagram or list views.

mentions.sessionTitle: Agentic infrastructure needs agentic observability
mentions.shortDescription: Agents reason over full system state rather than a curated slice, reducing hallucinated diagnoses
mentions.longDescription: groundcover proposes an architecture built for data abundance in which agents reason over complete system state rather than a curated slice or summary. The speaker argues that partial context is what creates hallucinated diagnoses, and that context quality matters as much as model quality, possibly more. This distinction separates an agent confidently hallucinating a fix from one that actually understands what is wrong.

mentions.sessionTitle: From zero to teammate in 25 minutes: Build a Teams agent live
mentions.shortDescription: Emoji reactions, targeted/private messages, slash commands, quoted replies, suggested actions, markdown support, and source citations are coming to agents in group chats (dedicated session the following day at 11:50).
mentions.longDescription: As a sneak peek ahead of a dedicated session the following day at 11:50, the team previews new capabilities for agents brought into group chats. These include emoji reactions so the agent can respond with emojis, targeted messages and slash commands enabling private messaging between the user and agent within a group chat, and quoted replies that let the agent quote a past message—useful for long-running tasks in busy group chats. Additional capabilities include suggested actions, markdown support, and source citations.

mentions.sessionTitle: Responsible AI in Action: From Principles to Real‑World Engineering
mentions.shortDescription: Default Microsoft guardrails can be extended with regex-based block lists (e.g., credit card patterns) and attached to an agent to block flagged queries directly
mentions.longDescription: The transcriptWindow contains only the speaker's introduction and general remarks about responsible AI and early agent building, with no detail on guardrails or block lists. Default Microsoft guardrails can be extended with custom block lists attached to an agent.

mentions.sessionTitle: Latest Cobalt VMs and Azure Boost enhancements​
mentions.shortDescription: Limited preview kicking off June 2026, enabling direct memory-to-memory transfers between VMs via the Microsoft Azure Network Adapter.
mentions.longDescription: Guest RDMA on Azure Boost enables direct memory-to-memory data transfers between VMs, demonstrated on a distributed AI inference workload using a prefill VM and a decode VM. Comparing RDMA versus TCP transport on the same model, prompts, and VMs, RDMA showed up to 2.2x higher throughput, a 3x reduction in time to first token, and roughly 20-25% faster token generation. The preview program kicks off in June 2026 as a limited preview to work closely with early customers, with a sign-up form available to join.

mentions.sessionTitle: Inside Azure innovations with Mark Russinovich
mentions.rawName: Guest VM-to-VM RDMA over Azure Boost
mentions.shortDescription: Demonstrated nearly doubling inference token throughput (3,400 to 7,637) and cutting median time-to-first-token from ~123k to ~47k ms in a disaggregated prefill/decode setup
mentions.longDescription: This brings RDMA to general-purpose workloads by enabling memory-to-memory transfers between virtual machines through Azure Boost, bypassing the TCP/IP and MANA (Microsoft Accelerated Network Adapter) driver stacks to eliminate memory copies and synchronization overhead. The demo targeted a common AI inference scenario that splits work into prefill (populating the KV cache from the prompt) and decode (generating new tokens), running each in separate server pools with different memory and compute constraints. Using a VLLM benchmark over TCP/IP first, the RDMA send-request stats stayed unchanged while throughput was measured, demonstrating the contrast with the RDMA path.

mentions.sessionTitle: GitHub Agentic Workflows: Automation That Actually Reads the Room
mentions.shortDescription: An accompanying Skills exercise built around a fictitious "Mona" website lets attendees reproduce the demo using their own GitHub handle.
mentions.longDescription: An accompanying GitHub Skills exercise lets attendees use their own GitHub handle to learn how agentic workflows work firsthand. The exercise centers on a fictitious Mona website tasked with looking at GitHub updates through blogs, change logs, and repository notes, then constantly generating updates that produce a pull request which can be merged directly or peer reviewed. Walking through the exercise in an issue, GitHub Agentic Workflows can automatically install itself and create a PR showing how to install it in the repository.

mentions.sessionTitle: Discover, govern, and scale Azure resources with HashiCorp Terraform
mentions.shortDescription: The discovery-to-import workflow can be set up programmatically through agentic loops.
mentions.longDescription: The discovery-to-import workflow can be set up in an almost programmatic way by bringing in the HashiCorp Terraform agent skills and using agentic loops. In the demo, four discovered resources generated about 300 lines of import statements and resource definitions, each with an import block below it to import the currently unmanaged resource into Terraform state via a single plan and apply cycle (also usable with HCP Terraform). After importing, the next step is applying organizational policies — such as a HashiCorp Sentinel policy — to eliminate drift and enforce tags, naming conventions, and SKUs.

mentions.sessionTitle: Claw and agent harness in Microsoft Foundry
mentions.shortDescription: A claw-like harness demonstrated running with a stateless, auto-shutdown back end (15-minute idle timeout) that uses Foundry models and Entra/Azure default credentials
mentions.longDescription: Hermes is a claw-like agent harness—it has memory, owns its environment (sandbox or VM), has tools and autonomy, can run for long periods, and connects to communication channels like Telegram or Slack—but it is not a literal fork or clone of Open Claw [inferred]. The speaker demonstrates Hermes running on Foundry hosted agents, which has a sandbox built in. The setup makes the agent always available while shutting down when idle so it isn't paid for continuously, and the speaker runs it in the terminal. It emphasizes a self-improving "collective wisdom" layer that gets better at your tasks the more you use it.

mentions.sessionTitle: Microsoft Build opening keynote
mentions.shortDescription: A fully managed, zone-redundant PostgreSQL service with 128 TB per cluster, 15 read replicas, and ~3x throughput over self-managed Postgres.
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft announced Horizon DB, a fully managed PostgreSQL service on Azure built ground-up for high-availability scale-out. It is zone-redundant with automated failover, offers 128 terabytes of storage per cluster, and supports 15 read replicas to scale read-heavy workloads. In internal testing, Horizon delivers roughly 3x throughput compared to any self-managed PostgreSQL setup. It is positioned to support the data-tier needs of agentic systems that continuously store, retrieve, reason, act, and learn.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: A server-side foundation for scaling and securely running agents
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft announced the host agent as a foundation for running agents on the server side. As agents increasingly need to run and scale, the open agent architecture executes on top of this host agent foundation so agents can be scaled and run securely. Offering this kind of environment is presented as a major point.

mentions.sessionTitle: Orchestrate omnichannel AI agents with Foundry and Twilio
mentions.shortDescription: Following Microsoft's public preview of hosted agents with WebSocket support and the Invocations API, TAC switched to a fully serverless deployment that gives each session its own dedicated sandbox, with scale-to-zero and no idle cost
mentions.longDescription: After finding that traditional compute with Container Apps—designed for stateless web services—wasn't built for the long-lived, stateful, per-user sessions that agents require, TAC switched to a hosted agents deployment option. Microsoft invested in hosted agents as a new compute primitive, recently going into public preview with WebSocket support and the Invocations API, which let TAC adopt it. The fully serverless option gives every session its own dedicated sandbox, predictable cold starts, scale-to-zero with no idle cost, state persistence, unique agent identity, and out-of-the-box observability, evaluations, and policies. In the new architecture, Twilio voice, SMS, and chat events flow over HTTP into an API Management Gateway that validates the Twilio signature, adds auth, and maps each Twilio conversation ID to a hosted agent session ID before routing into the sandbox, which connects to Azure Foundry for model inference.

mentions.sessionTitle: From prototype to production: build and run agents at scale
mentions.rawName: Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service (generally available soon)
mentions.shortDescription: Per-session sandbox isolation, sub-second cold start, zero idle-time cost, framework-agnostic, supporting long-running autonomous agents with durable state and file-system access
mentions.longDescription: Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service are becoming generally available soon, offering per-session sandbox isolation, sub-second cold start, zero idle-time cost, and a framework-agnostic design. Foundry hosted agents now even support long-running autonomous agents such as Open Claw [inferred] and Hermes agents, all with durable state execution and file-system access.

mentions.sessionTitle: Run AI SREs without burning token budgets
mentions.rawName: Hot context-window reuse leverages Anthropic's cache
mentions.shortDescription: Maintaining one context window per root cause lets retriggered investigations reuse a still-cached window (Anthropic's five-minute cache), making them far cheaper than a clean window.
mentions.longDescription: Yellin explains that with LLM-native grouping you effectively maintain one context window per root cause, so when new information arrives on a different alert and retriggers an investigation, you can reuse the previous context window. If that window is still hot—meaning still in Anthropic's five-minute cache hierarchy—reusing it is far cheaper than starting a clean context window. Applying these optimizations brings the per-investigation cost into a reasonable range, enabling teams to run AI SRE investigations on every single alert and have the agent automatically escalate important issues to humans.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build persistent and scalable AI agent memory with TiDB
mentions.rawName: Hybrid retrieval with RRF in one query
mentions.shortDescription: Vector and keyword searches run against the same table and are combined with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so rows ranking high in both lists win
mentions.longDescription: TiDB performs real hybrid search by combining two searches with a ranking step on top: one common table expression runs a vector search to grab the top 10 rows by meaning, while a second runs a keyword search to grab the top 10 by exact word match. The results are merged using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), so rows that rank high in both lists win. In the demo, asking about dietary restrictions returns the peanut allergy row first because it scores well in both the vector and keyword searches, all in one query against one database with no separate engines to keep in sync.

mentions.sessionTitle: Stop routing docstrings to 70B models with on-device AI on Snapdragon
mentions.shortDescription: A recreated Computex demonstration races Claude Opus 4.7 against a hybrid split (one hard task to cloud Opus, others to local models), producing identical output at roughly one-quarter the cost ($0.21 vs ~5.5 cents).
mentions.longDescription: A demo races two streams running the same prompt—designing a Snapdragon X2 Elite landing page with floating Taiwanese lanterns in the background—one running entirely on Claude Opus 4.7 in Anthropic cloud, the other in hybrid mode. In hybrid mode a classifier breaks the prompt into five tasks: one medium task needing up to a ~32B parameter model, three easy tasks runnable on a ~1B parameter model on the PC, and one hard task (the physics-based floating lanterns, requiring over a 70B parameter model) executed in the cloud on Opus 4.7. The cloud-only stream is expected to finish faster because the hybrid path is not yet optimized, though the speaker expects that to improve over time.

mentions.sessionTitle: Security for AI and Agent Augmented Coding on Windows
mentions.shortDescription: Hardware-level isolation with sub-second startup for higher-risk operations, demonstrated running PDF-annotation extraction via an mxc.exe [inferred] host process that leaves no traces.
mentions.longDescription: At the stronger end of the containment spectrum is the Hyperlight micro-VM, the execution primitive at the top of the agent containment stack, suited for higher-risk workloads that need a clearly isolated space while preserving the same agent experience. Micro-VMs are also about density, providing stronger separation without paying the full cost of a larger VM every time an agent runs. The demo follows Maya, a freelance interior designer using GitHub Copilot CLI, who asks Copilot in plain English to pull review comments from three client PDFs, group them by theme, and produce a prioritized summary—processed inside the micro-VM.

mentions.sessionTitle: Scalable Applications Without Polyglot tax: Azure SQL Hyperscale
mentions.rawName: Hyperscale named replicas with isolated working sets
mentions.shortDescription: Each named replica gets its own connection string, buffer pool, and RBPEX (Resilient Buffer Pool Extension) L2 cache, isolating read workloads from primary writes over the same up-to-128 TB dataset.
mentions.longDescription: A major advantage of Azure SQL Hyperscale is named replicas, where each readable copy gets its own connection string. Each named replica has its own buffer pool (memory) and L2 cache—called RBPEX, the Resilient Buffer Pool Extension—giving it its own working set that is distinct from any other named replica, while all share the same underlying dataset of up to 128 TB. This isolation lets writes on the primary remain unaffected by reads, so customers can run continuous writes on the primary while pointing agents at a named replica for vector distance and cosine similarity work.

mentions.sessionTitle: Microsoft Dataverse plugin: unleashing coding agents on the enterprise
mentions.shortDescription: The agent discovers the user's Dataverse environment from their Microsoft sign-in and configures the MCP server, requiring no org URL, config files, or setup docs.
mentions.longDescription: Because Maya [inferred] doesn't know her org URL and shouldn't have to, she connects using her Microsoft sign-in and issues a prompt asking the agent to connect her to her Dataverse environment. The agent discovers her environment from her Microsoft identity, configures the MCP server, and verifies the connection, all from one prompt with no pasted URL, config files, docs, setup, or guides. This lets her then describe and build a full data model in business terms.

mentions.sessionTitle: Under the hood of Microsoft AI models
mentions.shortDescription: Image generation and editing model ranked #2 for image-to-image on the LMArena [inferred] leaderboard, surpassing Nano Banana, with a Flash variant delivering production quality at roughly a third of the cost
mentions.longDescription: Image 2.5 is Microsoft AI's image generation and editing model, ranked #2 on the image editing leaderboard, surpassing Nano Banana. Its standout strength is precision: it executes edit instructions with high fidelity and consistency, handling complex compositional edits such as changing lighting, adding environment-matched objects, and editing one region while leaving the rest intact. The flagship model is optimized for maximum quality and is already live in PowerPoint, rolling out to OneDrive, and available on Foundry, while the Flash variant offers the same architecture tuned for high-volume production with more throughput and significantly lower cost per token. Users are encouraged to try it on the MAI Playground website, even from a phone.

mentions.sessionTitle: Union types in C#
mentions.rawName: Implicit conversions from case types to the union
mentions.shortDescription: case types convert automatically to the union type, while non-member types (e.g. a shark added to a list of pets) produce a compile error.
mentions.longDescription: Union types are created by typing `union` and listing the member types that make up the set (e.g. a union of pets). Case types can be implicitly converted to the union type, while non-member types produce a compile error—for example adding a shark to a list of pets yields "cannot implicitly convert type shark to pet." This provides type safety both when constructing a list and when switching over its values, which was not possible before with treating everything as object.

mentions.sessionTitle: Using autonomous SRE to move from alerts to action
mentions.shortDescription: An Intent Met quality score automatically calculated on every completed thread, rated on a one-to-five scale
mentions.longDescription: The Azure SRE Agent includes inbuilt evals such as the Intent Met quality score, which is automatically calculated on every completed thread and rated on a one-to-five scale so you can measure effectiveness over time. This sits alongside other monitoring capabilities including Session Insights for structured conversation summaries, an incident metrics dashboard showing mitigation rates and hours saved, and agent consumption tracking of Azure AI units used per day.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse
mentions.rawName: Inline Copilot in the SQL editor
mentions.shortDescription: AI assistance embedded directly in the query flow for joins, optimization, and natural-language-to-SQL.
mentions.longDescription: Copilot is now embedded directly inline in the SQL editor, placing AI assistance right in the developer's query flow. Whether you're stuck on a JOIN, want to optimize a query, or need to translate a business question into SQL, Copilot is available in context. This makes AI assistance feel like a true pair programmer rather than a bolt-on tool. It is part of a broader set of editor improvements including a new table overview page and streamlined query management.

mentions.sessionTitle: Microsoft Dataverse plugin: unleashing coding agents on the enterprise
mentions.shortDescription: The agent validates a security model by simulating each user's access and returning a pass/fail table, replacing manual private-browser impersonation.
mentions.longDescription: To validate a security model without juggling multiple browser sessions, Amara issues a prompt to validate the security model for each of Dakota, Lisa, and Mario, simulating their access and reporting whether they can read an account record, see a lifetime value, read a roast batch record, and read each other's business unit records, returned as a clear pass-fail table. The agent runs all 15 security validation tests inline and they pass, showing green check marks and red X's where each is expected. This replaces the usual manual process of logging in as each user in a private browser tab, confirming the configuration in seconds.

mentions.sessionTitle: Safeguard data across you apps and agents development cycle
mentions.rawName: Insider Risk Management support for agent-driven activity
mentions.shortDescription: IRM now tracks agent-triggered policy matches, generating alerts with full context just as it has for user-driven activity.
mentions.longDescription: Insider Risk Management (IRM), the solution within Purview, can now track and list risks for agent-driven activity in addition to the user-driven activity it previously supported. When an agent triggers a policy match, IRM generates an alert and provides a full picture to the security team, just as it did for user-risk-triggered policy matches. The alert detail shows the specific agent involved, the user who triggered the interaction, the risk severity, and the sequence of activities—including what data the agent accessed, whether sensitive content was present in prompts or responses, and whether any DLP policies were matched—helping security teams assess whether it is a real threat or a false positive.

mentions.sessionTitle: Designing Reliable Multi‑Agent Apps with Azure Cosmos DB
mentions.shortDescription: Generates embeddings asynchronously at write time via Microsoft Foundry integration, removing brittle synchronous calls to OpenAI
mentions.longDescription: Integrated embeddings automatically generate embeddings at write time, removing the brittle external synchronous call to OpenAI that could cause rate limiting or error handling issues before the conversation could continue. You write the raw message into Cosmos DB and it is automatically integrated with Microsoft Foundry, with embeddings generated asynchronously. You define your Microsoft Foundry integration and specify the source and target properties for the embeddings, giving full control without needing external pipelines or app-side coordination.

mentions.sessionTitle: Latest Cobalt VMs and Azure Boost enhancements​
mentions.shortDescription: Built on Intel Xeon 6 Granite Rapids with up to 15% CPU gains, scaling to 372 vCPUs and 2.8 TB memory.
mentions.longDescription: The Intel DSv7 and ESv7 series VMs are now generally available and are the first VMs to bring the latest generation of Azure Boost performance to customers. They are based on Intel's sixth-generation Xeon 6 Granite Rapids processor, delivering up to 15% CPU performance improvement over the prior generation, scaling up to 372 vCPUs and 2.8 TB of memory with turbo frequency up to 4.2 GHz. Running on Azure Boost servers, they reach up to 400 Gbps networking bandwidth, up to 800K IOPS and 20 GB/s throughput to premium V2/ultra remote storage, and up to 9.6 million IOPS and 53 GB/s throughput to local NVMe temp disk.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build and ship faster with a developer-optimized Windows experience
mentions.shortDescription: An experimental fork of Windows Terminal with integrated agents that analyze failed commands, suggest fixes, retain context across tabs, and connect to Copilot, Claude, or other agents on a permission-based model
mentions.longDescription: The Intelligent Terminal is an experimental fork of Windows Terminal that integrates agents directly into it. When a command errors out, it can analyze what happened and suggest a fix (e.g., adding a missing force attribute), or open an attached agent view where the user can ask it to fix issues; it retains context of commands run across all tabs. It comes with Copilot built in but can connect to Claude or other agents using the same protocol, and operates on a permission-based model requiring approval to access and run commands.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering enterprise-grade AI agents with Windows 365 for Agents
mentions.shortDescription: a dedicated experience under Devices > Windows 365 Cloud PCs lets admins create agent-specific pools with billing plans, always-available Cloud PCs, and gallery or custom images.
mentions.longDescription: Pool creation and assignment happen in Intune, where under Devices in Windows 365 Cloud PCs there is a dedicated experience for provisioning Cloud PCs specifically for agents. An admin creates a new provisioning policy by adding a name and description, selecting a billing plan for consumption-based charges, and associating a number of always-available Cloud PCs. Agent instances can be assigned to the policy as employees create them, and both custom and gallery images are supported along with a selectable language.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build Apps w/ Local AI for Unmetered Intelligence on every Windows PC
mentions.rawName: Ion [inferred] as successor to Phi Silica
mentions.shortDescription: A next-generation in-box model promising larger context windows, better quality, and faster tokens per second, already powering the Prompt API in Edge Canary.
mentions.longDescription: Ion, mentioned by Cynthia [inferred] in the keynote, will be the successor to Phi Silica and will be available via the AI APIs. It already powers the Prompt API in the Edge browser, which can be tried today by toggling a few flags in Edge Canary. Ion delivers bigger improvements in model quality, larger context window, and faster tokens per second, leveling up the language model experience of the AI APIs. Like the other APIs, Ion will be in-box, so Windows handles all distribution for developers.

mentions.sessionTitle: Unify your entire data estate on a single, AI-ready data lake
mentions.rawName: Item size reporting (preview) and lifecycle management with data tiering
mentions.shortDescription: New storage reporting plus the ability to move infrequently-used data into cool or cold tiers to lower storage costs.
mentions.longDescription: In public preview is new item size reporting, and as the biggest announcement, lifecycle management with data tiering is now available. New OneLake storage tiers and lifecycle management policies let users automatically move infrequently-used data into cool or cold tiers to save on storage costs, paying higher transaction prices only when the data is actually accessed. OneLake provides default tiering rules that can be customized.

mentions.sessionTitle: Profile and optimize agentic AI on Windows
mentions.shortDescription: Software traces are organized into structured domains (for example "OV phases") so AI models can be queried to generate breakdowns and reports
mentions.longDescription: Software traces, which are generally unstructured, are organized into structured domains so AI models can be run against them to produce analysis. In OpenVINO, the top-level layer captures the phases of execution under the "OV phases" domain name, so even with JSON output an AI model can be asked to look at the OV phases domain and generate a report and breakdown of the top level, then drill deeper. The goal is to organize software traces so they become friendly for AI and for future queries, enabling metrics like time to first token and decoding rate to be computed and then explored at operator or layer-level detail.

mentions.sessionTitle: From zero to teammate in 25 minutes: Build a Teams agent live
mentions.shortDescription: A `--json` flag returns structured output for scripting and agent parsing instead of human-formatted text.
mentions.longDescription: JSON mode is a CLI capability that returns structured output instead of human-formatted text. Commands like `teams app list` or get the app ID normally produce a nicely formatted, legible output for humans, but adding `--json` returns the same information in a structured format. This is powerful because the structured output can be used inside more complex scripts, letting agents pull values directly without having to parse human-readable text.

mentions.sessionTitle: Scale cloud-native workloads with Azure Linux
mentions.rawName: Kernel 6.18 maintained for the distribution lifetime
mentions.shortDescription: Azure Linux 4.0 ships the latest upstream kernel, to be maintained across the distribution's life.
mentions.longDescription: After SSHing into an Azure Linux 4.0 VM, the presenter showed it running kernel 6.18 [inferred] (transcribed as '618'), described as the latest upstream kernel that will be maintained for the lifetime of the distribution. The segment also highlighted security, with SELinux [inferred] enabled by default in enforcing mode out-of-the-box, and 'declarative deviations' that keep the image lean and optimized for Azure and cloud-native workloads.

mentions.sessionTitle: Turn your agents into action: Connect tools, APIs, and documents
mentions.rawName: Knowledge-source training for Extract, coming July
mentions.shortDescription: Customers can provide example documents so Content Understanding trains on and improves extraction for their specific forms.
mentions.longDescription: Coming in July, Content Understanding's Extract will ship a new training process using knowledge sources so customers can improve extraction on the documents that matter to them. If you have a specific document type—like a tax form or industry-specific financial document—you can provide example documents, and Content Understanding will train on them to improve its results. Alongside this, new prebuilt analyzers will offer significant token cost reductions for greater efficiency.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse
mentions.shortDescription: A diagnostic stored procedure (`sp_get_table_health_metrics` [inferred]) pinpoints root causes like fragmentation, small files, excessive deletes, or delayed checkpoints.
mentions.longDescription: Lakehouse table health checks address the challenge that lakehouse data queried through a SQL analytics endpoint isn't always in an optimal state, requiring manual maintenance as small files, fragmentation, and excessive updates and deletes build up. An official customer-facing diagnostic tool—a stored procedure referred to as "spgettablehealthmetrics" (sp_get_table_health_metrics [inferred])—lets you check table health with a single command and pinpoint the root cause, whether fragmentation, small files, too many deletes, or delayed checkpoints. It can be plugged into pipelines so table health is continuously monitored and maintenance happens proactively at scale.

mentions.sessionTitle: Designing Reliable Multi‑Agent Apps with Azure Cosmos DB
mentions.rawName: LangChain Azure Cosmos DB integration (generally available)
mentions.shortDescription: Packages the Cosmos DB vector store and LangGraph checkpointer store used to build the demo multi-agent app
mentions.longDescription: The LangChain Azure Cosmos DB integration is now generally available. It is an integration package that has all the Cosmos DB integration for LangChain and LangGraph used to build the multi-agent application. You can use the vector store integration from LangChain, and for state checkpointing in a multi-agent application you can use the LangGraph checkpointer store.

mentions.sessionTitle: Inside Azure innovations with Mark Russinovich
mentions.shortDescription: Now deployed across 30%+ of the fleet, reaching 400 Gbps networking (up from 200), 20 GB/s remote storage, 1M remote IOPS, and 6.6M local NVMe IOPS
mentions.longDescription: Azure Boost is an offload card that moves storage and networking data planes off the main server CPUs onto a card powered by DPUs, with ARM cores and an FPGA on the SoC where the data plane is processed and Microsoft's management agents run. The latest generation deploying in data centers reaches 20 GB/s remote storage, 1 million remote storage IOPS, 36 GB/s local NVMe storage [inferred], 6.6 million IOPS via NVMe offload acceleration, and 400 Gbps networking (up from 200) across two 200 Gbps ports supporting 400K connections per second. The dual ports connect to two top-of-rack switches for redundancy and sub-second servicing impact. Over 30% of the fleet now has Azure Boost enabled.

mentions.sessionTitle: Idea to production-ready agent in seconds on AI-native runtime
mentions.rawName: Layer 7 firewall and network isolation per sandbox
mentions.shortDescription: Operators can control which hosts and routes are allowed or denied for each agent
mentions.longDescription: Sandboxes are a controlled entity providing not just process isolation but also network isolation. Each sandbox includes a Layer 7 firewall that lets operators isolate all traffic and control exactly which hosts are allowed and which routes on which hosts are denied. In the demo, the agent Nova also inherited connectors for calendar, email, and Teams access from its sandbox group.

mentions.sessionTitle: So you want to become an MVP?
mentions.shortDescription: Staff directed attendees to aka.ms/mvp/learn for details on the program and how to contribute.
mentions.longDescription: Attendees are directed to aka.ms/mvp/learn to learn more about the MVP program and how to contribute. The speaker emphasizes that you don't need to be a Microsoft person—you can be an expert in open source or content creation—and that there is always a way to contribute, whether through blogs, videos, or other community-engaging activities.

mentions.sessionTitle: Develop faster on Windows with AI playbooks and local agents
mentions.shortDescription: Lemonade can directly launch agentic frameworks such as Codex, Claude, Gaia, or Open Claude and pair them with locally-runnable models.
mentions.longDescription: Lemonade, AMD's tool within the ROCm [inferred] stack that provides routing and abstraction over the backend (so developers don't need to be ROCm, HIP, GPU, NPU, or CPU experts), gained a new launch feature that plugs into the agentic layer. With it you can ask Lemonade to launch your favorite agentic framework—such as Codex, Claude, Gaia, or Open Claude [inferred]—making these tools interchangeable. Launching pulls up a list of client-centric default models that Lemonade routes to the local processor, choosing GPU for GGUF [inferred] files, NPU for Vitis or fast-flow stack models, and CPU otherwise.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build realtime multimodal agents with LiveKit and Azure
mentions.rawName: Live demo of a completed Build assistant
mentions.shortDescription: A customized agent greets the user and correctly answers that Microsoft Build 2026 runs June 2–3 in San Francisco at Fort Mason, with an online experience.
mentions.longDescription: A customized agent with a Microsoft Build themed front end greets the user warmly and offers help with Microsoft technologies like Azure, Windows, Microsoft 365, and GitHub. When asked for the dates, the computer voice correctly answers that Microsoft Build 2026 takes place June 2nd and June 3rd, a two-day event in San Francisco at Fort Mason with an online experience. The demo uses Azure STT and Azure TTS with a defined voice, plus a Solero [inferred] (Silero) VAD model, started in dev mode.

mentions.sessionTitle: Understand and fix Agent Framework apps with observability and evals
mentions.rawName: Live demo of a procurement evaluator agent built in ~11 lines
mentions.shortDescription: A line-of-business agent built on Microsoft Foundry with an OpenAI model, instructions, and tools that approves or denies purchase requests, illustrating how little code Agent Framework requires.
mentions.longDescription: Jim Bennett demonstrates an agent defined in roughly 11 lines of code consisting of an LLM, instructions, and tools — the components the speaker says literally make an agent. It uses an OpenAI model running on Microsoft Foundry, with instructions making it a procurement system evaluator that reads purchase requests, gathers relevant policy, vendor, and budget data, and approves or denies them. Tools include a check-policy tool and a tool to look up vendors and budgets. With Agent Framework, the developer interacts with the agent via a single line of code (agent run with inputs), and the framework handles the rest, though the speaker stresses it behaves as a black box.

mentions.sessionTitle: Beyond REST: .NET Apps That Talk to Hardware
mentions.rawName: Live NFC test-harness demo against remote hardware
mentions.shortDescription: Copilot ran an Android NFC test against two phones physically connected to a Mac mini in the speaker's basement, exercising reader/writer roles and packet comparison; the test returned false because the phones were intentionally mis-stacked
mentions.longDescription: The speaker ran a live demo asking Copilot to run the Android NFC test harness against hardware physically located in his basement, streamed to the audience. The setup centers on a Mac mini that the speaker logged into, with two phones physically connected for the NFC tests, plus Raspberry Pis connected over console; iOS is driven via a Python file and Android via ADB. The harness deploys the apps to the phones and attaches to them through the test harness to send commands. The test was expected to return false because the two phones were intentionally stacked incorrectly.

mentions.sessionTitle: Scale agentic AI cost‑efficiently on Azure with Arm Cobalt VMs
mentions.shortDescription: A polyglot microservices shopping-cart application runs across mixed Cobalt 100 and Cobalt 200 nodes, with CPU-based LLM inference and a shopping agent executing entirely inside the AKS cluster
mentions.longDescription: The demo shows a cloud-native polyglot microservices shopping-cart application running across a cluster with mixed Cobalt 100 and Cobalt 200 nodes, with microservices on Cobalt 100 and the orchestration on the more capable Cobalt 200. The Cobalt 200 nodes perform CPU-based LLM inference without needing any external accelerators, with everything running locally inside the AKS [inferred] cluster so data never leaves and no third-party LLM is called. An orchestrated family of agents manages the inferencing entirely on CPU within the trusted, local cluster.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build realtime multimodal agents with LiveKit and Azure
mentions.rawName: LiveKit MCP docs server and skill
mentions.shortDescription: Recommended as the most important tooling so coding agents build against up-to-date LiveKit context, given near-weekly feature shipping.
mentions.longDescription: The speaker recommends using the LiveKit MCP docs server or the skill as the most important tooling to ensure coding agents build against up-to-date LiveKit context. Because LiveKit ships new features almost every week and the docs are always kept current, a coding agent needs the most complete context to build accurately. The speaker prefers the MCP server for this purpose.

mentions.sessionTitle: Understand and fix Agent Framework apps with observability and evals
mentions.rawName: LLM-as-a-judge evals to test non-deterministic output
mentions.shortDescription: A scored rubric prompt converts non-deterministic agent output into a deterministic supported/unsupported verdict, revealing the demo agent passed only ~50% of cases.
mentions.longDescription: Evals are described as the AI term for testing — using an AI to judge whether the system is working, since AI can run at scale and doesn't get bored like human reviewers. The speaker writes a prompt that audits the automated procurement evaluator, showing each purchase request and deciding whether the recommendation is supported by the tool evidence alone, scored with a rubric (approve, reject, flag for review) and filling in the original request, the tool evidence, and the agent's reasoning. The prompt returns a single word — supported or unsupported — converting the non-deterministic AI output into a deterministic test result. This is run by downloading the telemetry data from Phoenix, pulling out the tool outputs, and passing them through the eval prompt.

mentions.sessionTitle: Run AI SREs without burning token budgets
mentions.rawName: LLM-native alert grouping delivers the largest savings
mentions.shortDescription: Since most alerts during an outage are duplicates of one root cause, letting the LLM generate and persist grouping rules avoids linear per-alert cost while avoiding the pitfalls of deterministic rules.
mentions.longDescription: Yellin identifies the biggest optimization as the fact that most alerts are duplicates; in a big production outage, the 500 incoming alerts are mostly duplicates of the same cause, so investigating each one naively incurs a linear cost. Grouping dramatically reduces this, but it must be LLM-native rather than using old-school deterministic rules, which either group too aggressively (merging different root causes) or not aggressively enough (missing alerts with different names from different systems). Their approach lets the LLM generate the grouping rules, persist them for a period, and control the policy on what triggers reinvestigations.

mentions.sessionTitle: Azure Storage for AI workloads​
mentions.shortDescription: A plugin offloads KV cache blocks from the open-source LMCache layer directly to durable blob storage for use with vLLM.
mentions.longDescription: LMCache is the open-source KVCache layer widely used with vLLM, and the most immediate payoff of the Azure Blob NIXL backend is realized through it. Microsoft's plugin lets LMCache offload KV blocks straight to Blob, keeping the picture consistent across the stack so OSS developers land on Azure Blob via NIXL and LMCache while managed customers land on Azure Context Cache. In a demo, an inference app on vLLM serving LLaMA 3.3 70B [inferred] is tensor parallel across four GPUs, with LMCache sitting alongside vLLM to build the KV cache and offload it to durable Azure storage.

mentions.sessionTitle: Security for AI and Agent Augmented Coding on Windows
mentions.rawName: Local capabilities discovery with detection hooks
mentions.shortDescription: Hooks before/after tool use and at prompt submission give security products like Microsoft Defender stable integration points to inspect and block threats such as indirect prompt injection.
mentions.longDescription: Local capabilities discovery gives developers and administrators a source of truth about what agent capabilities are present, enabled, allowed, and being used, and makes those actions admin-manageable to complement the security provided by containers. One of its most powerful additions is better detection and response: hooks before tool use, after tool use, and at prompt submission create stable integration points for security products like Microsoft Defender to inspect, evaluate, and respond. That consistent inspection is essential for enterprise customers to mitigate risks like indirect prompt injection, illustrated by a developer asking GitHub Copilot to fix a reported repo issue that hides a prompt injection attack in an attachment.

mentions.sessionTitle: AI Building Blocks for .NET: Add intelligence to your C# apps
mentions.shortDescription: The chat abstraction works identically with Ollama, LM Studio, or Foundry Local, demonstrated swapping models like Phi-4-mini for sentiment analysis
mentions.longDescription: The same chat abstraction that connects to cloud models in Azure also works identically with local model runtimes. The speaker demonstrates running local models via Ollama (on port 11434), noting you can equally use LM Studio or Foundry Local. A demo creates an Ollama chat client using Phi-4-mini to analyze the sentiment of a set of sentences and produce an overall average sentiment, all running locally with the same interface.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build AI-powered collaboration on a visual canvas
mentions.rawName: Lucid AI in the Lucidspark whiteboard
mentions.shortDescription: AI powers mind-map expansion, idea/sticky-note generation, sorting, and board summarization for collaborative ideation.
mentions.longDescription: Lucid AI in the Lucidspark whiteboard tool focuses on idea generation, starting with the Mindmap widget that can expand on ideas from a topic and keep branching into sub-topics. The Lucid AI Brainstorm tool's Generate Ideas section can produce sets of sticky notes and generate further ideas based on a selected note. Users can also take existing sticky notes and summarize them or sort them into high-level categories using the Sort tool.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build AI-powered collaboration on a visual canvas
mentions.shortDescription: An MCP server lets AI agents search, fetch, summarize, share, and create Lucid diagrams, with more tools described as coming in the pipeline.
mentions.longDescription: With Lucid's MCP server, AI agents can easily search, fetch, summarize, share, and create Lucid diagrams, with many more AI tools described as coming in the pipeline. Example use cases include funneling a meeting conference transcript into Lucid to build a process diagram, ideating with an LLM to design a workshop and create a Lucidspark board shared only with attendees, and connecting an agent to do a system check or sync updates between code and diagrams. The speaker then demonstrates a specific example using a code-based BPMN converter from GitHub that needs review by the security compliance team.

mentions.sessionTitle: Apply orchestration patterns for production AI agents
mentions.rawName: Maestro Case for complex exception-driven processes
mentions.shortDescription: a canvas where stages activate dynamically via case-manager rules or agent reasoning, supporting parallel work, re-entry, and escalations without explicit arrows.
mentions.longDescription: Maestro Case is a new canvas purpose-built for the dynamic, exception-driven work done in enterprises, going beyond straight-line BPMN. A Case Manager sits on top, with the case organized into stages and tasks (agents, API workflows, RPA, BPM, and external agents) under each. After the intake stage there are no arrows; each stage is activated based on what the case manager decides, either via rules or agent reasoning, supporting rework, parallel work such as underwriting and escalation running at once, re-entering stages, and escalations without losing continuity.

mentions.sessionTitle: Apply orchestration patterns for production AI agents
mentions.rawName: Maestro Flow, a new developer canvas
mentions.shortDescription: a visual canvas backed by the Maestro runtime with a schema natively supported by coding agents, allowing local files, Git version control, and inline agent configuration.
mentions.longDescription: Maestro Flow is a new developer-friendly visual canvas whose runtime is Maestro, providing the same enterprise-grade governance, auditability, and durability. Unlike similar visual layers, this canvas comes with a schema that is natively supported by coding agents, so an agent can write the entire file and affect everything in Flow. In Visual Studio Code, the local files for Flow live on the developer's machine, allowing use of any coding agent and review of changes via Git or other version control.

mentions.sessionTitle: Under the hood of Microsoft AI models
mentions.shortDescription: First Microsoft reasoning model: mixture-of-experts, 35 billion active parameters, ~1 trillion total, 256K context, hill-climbed from scratch with no distillation
mentions.longDescription: Thinking 1 is Microsoft's first reasoning model, given an in-depth look in this session. Its architecture is a mixture-of-experts model with 35 billion active parameters, about 1 trillion total, and a 256K context window, and it punches above its weight class on benchmarks. It was hill-climbed entirely from scratch with no distillation and no teacher model, using clean, commercially licensed data lineage suited for shipping to enterprise customers. Training used 30 trillion tokens processed in house plus another 3.55 trillion tokens of curated STEM, math, and coding data in mid-training, which also extends context to 256K.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: Next-generation in-house chips for AI processing (Maia) and Arm-based agent workloads (Cobalt), extending the line first announced three years prior
mentions.longDescription: Continuing server-side infrastructure innovation, Microsoft announced the Maia 200 and Cobalt 200, successors to the Maia and Cobalt chips first announced three years prior. Maia is a chipset designed to optimize AI processing, while Cobalt uses an Arm-based architecture optimized for agent applications. The emphasis is on executing workloads efficiently across both edge and infrastructure, framed around performance-per-watt and token efficiency.

mentions.sessionTitle: Using AI tools to teach old apps new tricks
mentions.rawName: Mainframe modernization added to GitHub Copilot Modernization
mentions.shortDescription: Reverse-engineers COBOL, JCL, and BMS into per-program documentation, then reimagines it as native Java with a native SQL data layer, delivered with partner experts
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft is introducing mainframe modernization as part of GitHub Copilot modernization to accelerate the overall mainframe modernization journey in a succinct, cautious, step-by-step manner. Starting in the modernize CLI, an assessment looks at source code such as COBOL, JCL, BMS, DB2, and VSAM files, identifies missing dependencies, and catches downstream issues early. It also documents the mainframe, providing a holistic executive-summary overview of what the application does, the user personas, functional modules, and key capabilities.

mentions.sessionTitle: Microsoft Build opening keynote
mentions.shortDescription: Next-generation topological qubit with a 20-second-to-one-minute mean lifetime (~1,000x Majorana 1) and one-microsecond operations.
mentions.longDescription: Satya Nadella announced Majorana 2, the next-generation topological qubit implementing a new material stack discovered, built, and fabricated with the help of Microsoft's discovery agentic loop. Its qubits are exceptionally reliable, providing a mean lifetime of 20 seconds up to a minute—about a thousand times higher than Majorana 1—while operations run in one microsecond, enabling complex quantum computation within that lifetime. It retains the same qubit form factor as Majorana 1 at one one-hundredth of a millimeter, controlled all digitally, making it possible to fit a million qubits on a chip smaller than a credit card. With Majorana 1 having proven the foundational physics, Majorana 2 begins the engineering scale phase.

mentions.sessionTitle: Move from data to intelligence with Oracle MCP and Microsoft IQ
mentions.rawName: Managed, hosted Oracle MCP servers for Oracle Database@Azure
mentions.shortDescription: Oracle offers native, managed MCP servers in both Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and for databases running at Azure, with the MCP server itself provided at no additional cost (customers pay only for database and AI tooling usage).
mentions.longDescription: Oracle now offers managed, hosted MCP servers natively in both Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and for Oracle Databases running at Azure. Customers or partners can define the characteristics of the MCP server—what tools are made available and how authentication works—and Oracle runs it for them at no additional cost. The only charges are for using the database or the AI tooling; the MCP server itself is free. Setup begins with defining a database connection using a set of credentials (such as a proxy user tied to an identity domain) that shape what data the AI can see.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build the thing that builds the thing
mentions.shortDescription: Spins up boxes to record video of a bug and its fix, verifying the change so the maintainer only watches the video and merges.
mentions.longDescription: Mantis is an agent the speaker can ping on a pull request that spins up Crab Box instances to make a video of the bug, fix it, make a video of the fix, and actually look at the videos to verify the change. It builds on earlier work adding VNC and screenshot/click/type computer automation to Crab Box so the agent can drive a UI itself. The end-to-end flow lets him ping Clause Reaper [inferred] to create the PR, have Mantis do the visual verification, and then simply watch the video and merge.

mentions.sessionTitle: Taking your AI to the edge with .NET MAUI
mentions.shortDescription: Pin clustering, custom image-source pins, map interactions, and Android JSON styling
mentions.longDescription: The .NET MAUI 11 maps control, which renders to Apple Maps on iOS and Google Maps on Android, gains several enhancements beyond its previous basic functionality. New capabilities include pin clustering with steerable grouping behavior, custom pins specified simply via an image source rather than custom handlers, map interactions such as long press, and Android-specific JSON styling customization. These additions round out previously missing functionality in the control.

mentions.sessionTitle: GitHub Agentic Workflows: Automation That Actually Reads the Room
mentions.shortDescription: Workflows are authored as Markdown files (optionally generated with Copilot) and compiled into a YAML "lock file" that GitHub Actions runs.
mentions.longDescription: Instead of having to know YAML for GitHub Actions, developers can define their workflows in Markdown, and can even use Copilot to create those Markdown files, which are then compiled into an agentic workflow. This addresses how traditional automation and CI is rigid and prone to syntax errors that are hard to identify. The agentic approach makes it easier to automate CI/CD, triage test failures, create issues, produce daily reports, and open pull requests.

mentions.sessionTitle: Taking your AI to the edge with .NET MAUI
mentions.shortDescription: A vehicle for faster experimental releases including DevFlow, Essentials.AI, AI extensions, and new Linux/macOS AppKit/WPF backends
mentions.longDescription: MAUI Labs is a new initiative created as a vehicle to release experimental things faster, acknowledging that not everything will stick but inviting the community to try, contribute ideas, and collaborate. It includes DevFlow, a companion that lets Copilot see and verify the application to work more effectively, and Essentials.AI, which follows the .NET MAUI paradigm to use on-device AI services like Apple Intelligence, Gemini on Android, and Phi Silica on Windows, plus local and remote models. AI extensions exploring new in-app navigation are also part of the effort.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build persistent and scalable AI agent memory with TiDB
mentions.rawName: MCP server and agent rules for AI coding tools
mentions.shortDescription: Published for Cursor and Claude users to integrate TiDB into coding workflows
mentions.longDescription: For Cursor and Claude users, TiDB provides an MCP server along with a bunch of agent rules available on GitHub at github.com/pinkapp/agentrules [inferred]. These let developers drop TiDB directly into their AI coding workflow.

mentions.sessionTitle: Move from data to intelligence with Oracle MCP and Microsoft IQ
mentions.rawName: MCP servers for Oracle AI Database since July
mentions.shortDescription: Oracle has shipped MCP server support for its AI Database, extending now into cloud-hosted managed offerings.
mentions.longDescription: Jeff Smith notes that Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerged in late 2024 and gained rapid adoption throughout 2025. Oracle has had MCP servers for Oracle AI Database since July, and is now extending support to cloud-hosted managed offerings in both Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and for Oracle Databases running at Azure.

mentions.sessionTitle: Accelerating developer productivity with Windows 365
mentions.shortDescription: A set of Model Context Protocol tools lets any MCP-speaking agent framework provision, connect to, interact with, and manage the lifecycle of a Cloud PC, managed through the Agent 365 portal.
mentions.longDescription: Windows 365 for Agents includes an MCP tool layer built on the Model Context Protocol, the open standard for connecting agents to tools. Microsoft ships a set of MCP tools that let an agent provision a Cloud PC, connect to it, interact with it, and manage its lifecycle, so any agent framework that speaks MCP works with Windows 365 for Agents. The MCP tools are managed through the Agent 365 portal, with observability and governance surfacing the same way as for any Agent 365-enabled agent, while Cloud PC pools are managed in Intune and identity goes through Entra ID. Integration is demonstrated using the A365 toolkit and a tooling manifest that declares which MCP servers the agent can access.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering enterprise-grade AI agents with Windows 365 for Agents
mentions.rawName: MCP tool layer for Cloud PCs
mentions.shortDescription: a set of Model Context Protocol tools lets any MCP-speaking agent framework provision, connect to, interact with, and manage the lifecycle of a Cloud PC.
mentions.longDescription: Windows 365 for Agents ships an MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool layer, using the open standard for connecting agents to tools. The set of MCP tools lets an agent provision a Cloud PC, connect to it, interact with it, and manage its lifecycle. If an agent framework speaks MCP, it works with Windows 365 for Agents.

mentions.sessionTitle: Multi-agents in action with 3 AI agents, 3 frameworks, tools & models
mentions.rawName: Memory and disk snapshots with sub-second resume
mentions.shortDescription: Idle sandboxes are snapshotted (file system and memory), stop incurring compute cost, and resume in under a second.
mentions.longDescription: Sandboxes support snapshots not just for disk but also for memory, allowing idle sandboxes to be preserved and restored to a previous point. This is useful for long running tasks where you want to preserve state, and the infrastructure resumes instantly so agents don't wait on cold starts. The capability enables bursting to hyperscale while maintaining state across tool calls.

mentions.sessionTitle: .NET 11 in depth: Runtime, libraries, and SDK for the AI era
mentions.shortDescription: A two-release effort redefining the `unsafe` keyword as a reviewable caller contract and reducing unsafe usage, including in SIMD code
mentions.longDescription: Memory safety is a massive two-release project spanning .NET 11 and 12, in preview in .NET 11. In this release the team is defining a set of language changes, applying them to System.Private.CoreLib (the bottom-most managed library), and making changes so they and others need to use Unsafe less, including in SIMD code. The key takeaway, detailed in a blog post written about a week prior, is that the Unsafe keyword is being redesigned to mean a reviewable caller contract rather than establishing an unsafe context, with APIs like Unsafe and MemoryMarshal marked with this contract; .NET 12 finishes the work.

mentions.sessionTitle: Inside Azure innovations with Mark Russinovich
mentions.shortDescription: Launched 10,000 sandboxes with a ~2-second average launch time
mentions.longDescription: To make lightweight container sandboxes start almost instantaneously for agent workloads, ACI uses memory snapshotting: a container is started, its memory is snapshotted, and subsequent requests for the same container simply map that memory, skipping all initialization. The demo launched 10,000 container sandboxes using 10 workers each launching 1,000 sandboxes, completing with an average launch time of about 2 seconds, demonstrating both speed and scale. This capability underpins agent sandboxing landing on top of Azure Container Instances.

mentions.sessionTitle: Imagine Cup World Championship
mentions.shortDescription: The champion receives a one-on-one mentorship with Microsoft's Chairman and CEO.
mentions.longDescription: Dona Sarkar explained that the Imagine Cup grand prize includes $100,000 and a mentoring session with Satya Nadella himself. This mentorship was described as a key part of what was at stake for the competing founders.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse
mentions.shortDescription: Re-architected sync makes lakehouse data queryable in seconds rather than minutes.
mentions.longDescription: Rakesh Krishnan announces the public preview of a re-architected metadata sync for the SQL analytics endpoint that every Fabric lakehouse uses to query data with familiar SQL constructs. Historically there was a delay after data landed in the lakehouse before it could be queried, but the new version is built on a completely different architecture that increases sync performance and minimizes data staleness. As a result, data becomes available for query in seconds rather than minutes once it lands in the lakehouse.

mentions.sessionTitle: AI Building Blocks for .NET: Add intelligence to your C# apps
mentions.shortDescription: Adds an `IAgent` interface wrapping the chat client, supporting tools, agent orchestration patterns (sequential, round-robin), and workflows
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft Agent Framework adds a new IAgent interface layered on top of the chat client. After creating a chat client, you call create agent to produce a minimal agent defined by a name, description, and instructions—essentially a wrapper over the chat client that retains the same patterns and capabilities, including StreamingAsync. The framework also brings in related topics such as tools, agent orchestration, workflows, agent-to-agent connections, and durable functions/workflows. The demo defines a writer agent that writes a short story about a haunted house with a character named Lucia.

mentions.sessionTitle: From prototype to production: build and run agents at scale
mentions.shortDescription: Now includes a built-in harness integrated with skills, memory, and middleware, plus plug-in integrations for the GitHub Copilot SDK and Claude Agent SDK [inferred]
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft Agent Framework is now at version 1.0 and production ready. As Jeff demonstrated, it now has a built-in harness that is well integrated with skills, memory, and middleware. It also includes plug-in integrations with harnesses such as the GitHub Copilot SDK and the Claude Agent SDK [inferred].

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: Seven models presented by Mustafa Suleyman [inferred], including image (MAI Image 2.5 [inferred]) and a reasoning model (MAI Thinking [inferred]); plus frontier tuning for domain-specific optimization
mentions.longDescription: Presented by Mustafa Suleyman [inferred], founder of DeepMind and now leader of the Microsoft AI effort, Microsoft released seven different models. Examples include an image model (MAI Image 2.5 [inferred]) for image optimization and a high-accuracy character recognition model, with the most emphasized being a reasoning-based standard model (MAI Thinking [inferred]). Microsoft also presented frontier tuning, which optimizes a model using a company's own domain knowledge, all within the Microsoft Foundry that supports over 11,000 models.

mentions.sessionTitle: Embracing frontier R&D with Microsoft Discovery
mentions.shortDescription: A lightweight local on-ramp to frontier R&D that requires only a GitHub Copilot license and no Azure account to get started
mentions.longDescription: The Microsoft Discovery app is a lightweight, free on-ramp to frontier R&D that complements the core enterprise services. It is a free download that only requires a GitHub Copilot license to get started, and does not need an Azure account, though having one provides access to enterprise services. It is positioned to reduce the friction of configuring Azure resources and dealing with IT compliance for those who just want to explore agentic discovery.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: Research-exploration services for drug/chemical discovery and quantum computing progress targeting 2029. [00:20:00]
mentions.longDescription: Under the "Beyond the Frontier" theme, Microsoft announced Microsoft Discovery, now GA, a research-exploration service optimized for areas such as drug discovery and chemical substances, applying AI to generate and repeatedly test hypotheses. Microsoft also highlighted progress in quantum computing with the Majorana 2 [inferred] chip, improving reliability and minimizing error rates, with capabilities targeted to become reality in 2029.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: A sandboxed runtime for safely executing agent actions (e.g., the OpenClaw [inferred] computer-use agent), with native binaries and a TypeScript SDK published on GitHub. [00:09:43]
mentions.longDescription: The Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) is a sandboxed runtime that lets agents run safely and securely, used in keynotes to run OpenClaw [inferred] on Windows and also underpinning the Copilot SDK. MXC implements a native binary for the OS layer, and the SDK for the interface to that native binary is implemented in TypeScript. This is publicly available on GitHub as a preview of the service.

mentions.sessionTitle: Microsoft Build opening keynote
mentions.shortDescription: OS-native isolation/containment policy for agents; OpenClaw runs natively on Windows via MXC with a WinUI 3 companion app.
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft introduced Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), a new policy layer that lets Windows apply isolation and containment to agents using OS-native primitives baked into the operating system so containment is enforced by policy. Options range from process-level isolation for lightweight agent actions, session-level isolation for user separation, Windows and Linux VMs (including WSL) for stronger boundaries, to Windows 365 for agents for maximum isolation in a separate managed environment. Developers can pick the right containment option per workload and Windows enforces it via MXC, regardless of who built the agent. NVIDIA is bringing OpenClaw [inferred] to Windows to securely execute autonomous AI agents.

mentions.sessionTitle: Building Agents You Can Trust on Windows
mentions.shortDescription: A cross-platform, declarative library that dynamically composes a right-sized container per agent action by matching developer, user, and IT policy against available OS primitives.
mentions.longDescription: The Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) Library is introduced to create containers based on policy, providing an isolation boundary proportionate to the risk and action an agent performs. Developers and agents declare the security requirements of the agent and its individual actions, and the library compiles those and matches them against system policies and policies defined by IT through familiar deployment, management, and monitoring tools. Once a match occurs, the MXC library examines the native OS platform primitives and assembles the right container for the job, a process called dynamic composition. This enables least-privilege enforcement where each action runs in its own sandbox with policy defining just what it can do.

mentions.sessionTitle: Security for AI and Agent Augmented Coding on Windows
mentions.shortDescription: A single SDK and policy model that applies OS-enforced containment across multiple isolation primitives, so one coherent abstraction can cover many workload types.
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft introduced the Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) SDK, a single SDK that lets developers apply containment policies on agents that are enforced by the OS. It provides an abstraction layer across various isolation primitives, simplifying the containment of many different types of workloads. The SDK is built around a composable sandbox model so the same policy can map to different isolation boundaries depending on the workload, avoiding lock-in to one rigid container.

mentions.sessionTitle: AI Building Blocks for .NET: Add intelligence to your C# apps
mentions.shortDescription: The `IChatClient` interface lets the same code target cloud models in Foundry or local runtimes, with integrated Entra ID identity recommended over API keys
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft.Extensions.AI is presented as the foundation layer of the .NET AI building blocks—a provider-agnostic chat abstraction centered on the IChatClient interface. The same code can connect to a chat model running in the cloud (for example, in Foundry) or to another provider running locally. When using a backend like Foundry, instead of the standard endpoint URL, model name, and API key, you can use integrated identity and pass your Entra ID to authenticate, which is the recommended approach.

mentions.sessionTitle: Build smarter AI systems in Foundry as models and costs evolve
mentions.rawName: Microsoft first-party models live in Foundry
mentions.shortDescription: New MAI models, including MAI-Image 2.5 [inferred], went live during the morning keynote, spanning image, code, and audio for a full multimodal stack
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft announced new first-party MAI models during the morning keynote with Mustafa, and the team pushed them live during the session. These models span image, code, and audio, forming a full multimodal application stack. The speaker highlighted MAI-Image 2.5 [inferred] as one of the latest models, emphasizing efficient running and cost optimization.

mentions.sessionTitle: Under the hood of Microsoft AI models
mentions.shortDescription: Lets developers and organizations tune models on their own data inside their secure tenant, deploying through Foundry or Copilot
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft Frontier Tuning, announced at the morning keynote, lets every developer and organization build its own hill-climbing machine—a model trained on their own work, language, and data entirely inside their environment, rather than renting a generic model. It emphasizes four things: it is private so data never moves, cost efficient, gets smarter on the user's actual context, and keeps the user in control with no big-model lock-in. The process is to define the task and what good looks like, bring your data and M365, Azure, and Fabric context and workflows, then run training inside your secure tenant, deploying through either Foundry or Copilot. Real usage feeds back into the next training cycle so the model improves the more the organization uses it.

mentions.sessionTitle: Taking your AI to the edge with .NET MAUI
mentions.shortDescription: Builds on Microsoft.Extensions.AI to add on-device providers Apple Intelligence, Gemini Nano, and Windows Copilot Runtime via Phi Silica [inferred]
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft.Maui.Essentials.AI is a new library that builds on top of Microsoft.Extensions.AI, the unified API for working with any AI model whether local or remote without changing code. Essentials.AI adds on-device, on-machine AI providers including Apple Intelligence, Gemini Nano, and the Windows Copilot Runtime through Phi Silica, letting developers easily use local models across the platforms .NET MAUI reaches. It also supports switching to cloud providers such as Azure OpenAI and Foundry via interfaces like IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator, enabling AI-enabled apps with minimal effort.

mentions.sessionTitle: Responsible AI in Action: From Principles to Real‑World Engineering
mentions.rawName: Microsoft Purview for AI agent governance
mentions.shortDescription: Purview (renamed from compliance tooling because it now covers more than compliance) surfaces agent activity, sensitive data, and DSPM views, with AI interaction logs retained for 30 days
mentions.longDescription: The transcriptWindow contains only the speaker's introduction and high-level framing of responsible AI, with no specific detail about Purview. Microsoft Purview provides governance over AI agent activity, sensitive data, and DSPM views.

mentions.sessionTitle: Japan Wrap-up Session
mentions.shortDescription: An autonomous "Autopilot" agent demoed in Japanese performing expense reimbursement across M365 cloud and local data, with the final decision left to a human
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft Scout is an autonomous "Autopilot" agent, demonstrated in Japanese performing a business trip expense reimbursement task. It simultaneously searches M365 cloud data and local data to find files, analyzes them to extract reimbursement content, and enters the data into the user's usual expense application. The agent takes the lead but leaves the final decision to a human for safety and security, with Microsoft Scout uploading files and completing the settlement.

mentions.sessionTitle: Building WinUI Apps with C# First Patterns and AI Assisted Workflows
mentions.rawName: Microsoft UI Reactor experimental framework released
mentions.shortDescription: A new open-source, high-churn project for experimenting with new programming styles, controls, and app models, with proven ideas later pushed down into production WinUI.
mentions.longDescription: Microsoft UI Reactor is a newly announced experimental framework for experimenting with new styles of programming, new controls, and new app models. It is an open-source project, very early and with a high churn rate (code changing daily), intended as a place for community feedback, guidance, and participation, with PRs already landing from the community. As good ideas are found and baked, they will be pushed down into the production WinUI bits to become consistent and standard across the WinUI stack.

mentions.sessionTitle: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse
mentions.shortDescription: Live connectivity GA (no DACPAC extraction) and .SQL file input (public preview) supporting Azure Synapse, SQL Server, and any T-SQL source.
mentions.longDescription: The migration assistant is now generally available with enhancements that simplify modernizing data stacks and moving customers from their existing data warehouse to Fabric. Live connectivity is now GA, connecting directly to the source system and eliminating the need for DACPAC extraction or manual prep work. Support for .SQL files as input is going into public preview for bringing existing script schema definitions or workloads across without a live connection. The tool supports a broad variety of sources including Azure Synapse, SQL Server, or effectively any T-SQL database.

mentions.sessionTitle: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio: Agents That Debug, Profile, and Test
mentions.rawName: Migration to the GitHub Copilot CLI SDK
